Narrow nets are capacity-limited so additional L2 pushes them into underfitting.
Larger batches average out the gradient noise that a very high learning rate amplifies, stabilizing training.
Strong L2 slows fitting and more update steps per epoch from smaller batches help compensate within a fixed epoch budget.
Extra layers need more optimization progress, which a tiny learning rate cannot deliver in 243 epochs.
A single hidden layer relies on width for all its capacity, so widening substitutes for missing depth.
Wide layers make each Adam step change outputs much more, so a very high learning rate becomes unstable.
With tiny batches updates are already numerous and noisy, so a higher learning rate pushes training into instability.
Very wide nets are already fast learners and more sensitive to step size, so raising the learning rate overshoots sooner.
